purpose: Scores each credit-card client with the probability of defaulting on the next month's payment (the notebook calls it the "Traditional Score"), using credit limit, demographics, recent repayment status and recent payment amounts.
intended_use: Not stated in the source or documents. The notebook is an exploratory comparison of scoring approaches on a public dataset; it names no business decision, cut-off policy or user. Governance fields must come from the model owner.
out_of_scope_use: The evidence defines no permitted use. Based on what the code does, it should not be used for any population other than the one it was fitted on (Taiwan credit-card clients, April 2005 to September 2005), nor for new-applicant origination, because every strong input is account behaviour that a new applicant does not have.
methodology: Binomial generalised linear model with a logit link (logistic regression), fitted by R's glm on a stratified training partition. Categorical inputs (sex, education, marriage) enter as treatment-coded dummies against their first level; repayment status variables enter as linear numeric terms; credit limit and payment amounts enter untransformed. Scores are predicted probabilities on the response scale for the test partition.
target_definition: default.payment.next.month: binary flag for whether the client defaults on the payment due in the month after the observation window. Converted to a factor before fitting, so the model estimates the probability of the second level (1 = default).

variables.name: limit_bal
variables.description: Amount of given credit (credit limit) on the card.

variables.name: sex
variables.transformation: Converted to a factor; level 1 (male) is the reference.

variables.name: education
variables.description: Highest education level (sensitive; proxy for socio-economic status).

level_meaning.4: others (includes merged undocumented and unknown codes)

variables.transformation: Codes 0, 4, 5 and 6 merged into 4, then converted to a factor; level 1 (graduate school) is the reference.

variables.name: marriage
variables.transformation: Code 0 merged into 3, then converted to a factor; level 1 (married) is the reference.

variables.name: pay_0
variables.description: Repayment status for the most recent month of the observation window: months of payment delay.
variables.transformation: Codes -2, -1 and 0 merged into 0 (paid / not late); kept numeric, so each extra month of delay has the same linear effect on the log-odds.

variables.name: pay_2
variables.description: Repayment status two months before the most recent month: months of payment delay.
variables.transformation: Codes -2, -1 and 0 merged into 0; kept numeric (linear term).

variables.name: pay_3
variables.description: Repayment status three months back: months of payment delay.
variables.transformation: Codes -2, -1 and 0 merged into 0; kept numeric (linear term).

variables.name: pay_5
variables.description: Repayment status five months back: months of payment delay.
variables.transformation: Codes -2, -1 and 0 merged into 0; kept numeric (linear term).

variables.name: pay_6
variables.description: Repayment status six months back (oldest month in the window): months of payment delay.
variables.transformation: Codes -2, -1 and 0 merged into 0; kept numeric (linear term).

variables.name: pay_amt1
variables.description: Amount of the most recent previous payment.

variables.name: pay_amt2
variables.description: Amount of the previous payment one month earlier.

variables.name: default.payment.next.month
variables.description: Default on next month's payment (1 = default, 0 = no default).
variables.transformation: Converted to a factor; used to stratify the train/test partition.

preprocessing.description: Read the raw CSV and lower-case all column names.
preprocessing.author_rationale: Author put the column names to lower case for convenience.

preprocessing.description: Drop the client identifier column id.
preprocessing.author_rationale: id is the client identifier and carries no meaning for the model.
Codes outside the data definition, and the 'unknown' codes, are not meaningful on their own.
Code 0 is not in the data definition.

preprocessing.description: For the six repayment-status columns, selected by position (columns 6 to 11 after id is dropped: pay_0, pay_2, pay_3, pay_4, pay_5, pay_6), merge codes -2, -1 and 0 into 0.
preprocessing.author_rationale: Many -2 and 0 values appear that the data definition does not explain; the author assumes -2, -1 and 0 all mean the account is not late.

preprocessing.description: Convert sex, education, marriage and the target to factors; repayment status stays numeric.
preprocessing.author_rationale: pay_x could be treated as factors but the author keeps them numeric.

preprocessing.description: Stratified random partition on the target: 70% training, 30% test, using caret::createDataPartition with no seed.
preprocessing.author_rationale: Hold out a test set to compare models.

variable_selection: The notebook first fits a logistic model on all columns (formula with '.'), then fits the final model on a hand-picked subset of eleven inputs. The selection criterion is not written down; the supporting document only shows that the full model was summarised before the subset was chosen. age, pay_4, bill amounts and older payment amounts were available but excluded.
assumptions: Repayment status codes -2, -1 and 0 mean the same thing (not late); stated by the author as an assumption, not taken from the data definition.
Undocumented education codes (0, 5, 6) and the 'unknown' codes belong with 'others'; undocumented marriage code 0 belongs with 'others'.
Months of payment delay act linearly on the log-odds (repayment status kept numeric rather than categorical).
Payment amounts and credit limit act linearly on the log-odds with no transformation or capping.
The stratified random partition is representative of the population the score will be applied to; there is no out-of-time test.

limitations.text: Sex and marital status (marriage) are direct model inputs. Using protected characteristics in a credit decision needs explicit legal justification under the Equality Act 2010 and a fairness assessment; the source gives no justification.
Education is a direct input. It is not a protected characteristic in itself but is a likely proxy for socio-economic status and age, so it must be included in the fairness assessment.

The train/test split is random and the legacy source sets no seed, so the published model, its coefficients and its reported test metrics cannot be reproduced exactly. The factory's capture harness fixed a seed to obtain a reference run; that run is a reproduction, not the original.

Category codes are merged before fitting: education 0/4/5/6 into 4, marriage 0 into 3, and repayment status -2/-1/0 into 0. The repayment merge rests only on the author's assumption and discards the distinction between 'pay duly' and the undocumented codes; the education merge pools undocumented codes with 'others', which can create a spurious coefficient for that group.
Several terms in the final model are not statistically significant (education2, education3, marriage3, pay_2), yet the model keeps them; the variable selection rule is undocumented.
The repayment-status columns are selected by position (columns 6 to 11) rather than by name, so any change in column order of the input file silently recodes the wrong variables.
Repayment delay is fitted as a linear numeric term; the effect of moving from 0 to 1 month late is forced to equal the effect of moving from 7 to 8 months late.
The legacy source defines no decision cut-off. The supporting notebook picks the cut-off that maximises accuracy on the test set, which uses test data for tuning and has no business or cost basis.
Data covers Taiwan credit-card clients from April 2005 to September 2005; representativeness for any current portfolio is not established and there is no out-of-time validation.
Parts of the legacy source are marked [reconstructed]: the education and marriage recodes and the factor conversions were described in the notebook text but their code was not printed.

code_vs_docs_discrepancies: The education and marriage recodes and the factor conversions (lines marked [reconstructed]) are described in the notebook prose but their code is not shown; the legacy script reconstructs them from that prose.
The notebook's data definition lists education 5 and 6 as 'unknown' and does not mention code 0; the code merges all of 0, 4, 5 and 6 into 'others' rather than keeping an 'unknown' group.
The notebook scores test.x (the test set without the target column); the legacy script scores test.batch directly. The predictions are identical because the target is not a model input.
The notebook also builds challenger models (for example a decision tree with rpart) and computes the accuracy-maximising cut-off; the legacy script contains only the logistic 'Traditional Score'.
open_questions: What business decision does this score support, and who owns it? (The evidence names none.)
What was the variable selection criterion for the final eleven inputs, and why was age excluded while sex and marital status were kept?
Is there a documented legal justification for using sex and marital status as inputs, or should a variant without them be built?
What do repayment status codes -2 and 0 mean in the source system? The author's merge with -1 is unverified.
Which cut-off, if any, is used in production, and on what data was it set?
Was the original model fitted with a recorded seed or saved split that would allow exact reproduction?
